items.title: [Christopher Roosen] Current Forms of AI Are Very Unlikely To Be Conscious and the Concern is a Distraction From Crucial Technology Design Questions
items.content_html: Philosopher Thomas Nagel once proposed, using a bat’s inner life as a thought experiment, that we can’t ever really know what it’s like to experience the world as anyone but ourselves. Put another way, Nagel proposed consciousness is entirely subjective, private and unknowable. A version of this idea is being used to argue Large Language Model-based systems might be conscious and self-aware. However, based on the evidence so far, this seems a spurious claim and a distracting question from deeper design concerns.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] What happens when people have to jump in to clean up AI’s mess?
items.content_html:
🎨 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Imagine an artificial intelligence system that has performed reliably for months. Its recommendations are almost always right, and the employee reviewing them has learned that close scrutiny rarely changes the outcome. Then something unusual happens. The AI makes an error or can’t proceed and needs human intervention. The employee is expected to step in and remains responsible for the outcome.

But does the employee know how to do the task?

I’m a professor of management information systems and the academic director of Drexel University’s Center for Applied AI & Business Analytics. In my research on human-AI relationships, I call this latent risk: the possibility that people may lose capabilities their organizations still depend on them to exercise.

AI can continue to perform well while the people overseeing it become less practiced at exercising independent judgment and less prepared to intervene. The risk becomes latent when the organization still depends on that human capability to step in but has little cause to notice that that capability may be weakening.

The concern is not entirely new. The idea of latent risk builds on decades of research into how people respond to automation. For example, studies of automation bias have shown that people can miss problems or follow automated recommendations even when other evidence suggests they should not.

What is different today is the role AI is beginning to play in organizations. It is beginning to assume larger parts of the analysis and decision-making that people previously performed.

Human in the loop explained.

The success paradox

The better AI becomes, the more the nature of human work changes. Work that once required an employee to analyze a problem and reach a decision may instead be performed by AI, leaving the employee to review its recommendation. The employee is no longer doing the same work with AI assistance—rather, their job has shifted from doing the work to overseeing what the AI does.

This shift is already beginning to change how some companies train employees. Accounting giant Deloitte, for example, is redesigning its graduate audit training as AI takes over some of the manual work traditionally done by junior auditors. The firm is introducing simulations so trainees can still develop the judgment they will need as they move into more complex work.

More than four decades ago, cognitive psychologist Lisanne Bainbridge described one of the “ironies of automation”: As systems take over more of the work, instead of simply having their work loads lightened, people can be left facing new challenges in monitoring the systems and handling the unusual situations the systems cannot. Later studies found another problem: As people become less involved in a task, they can become less prepared to step in when needed. Researchers have called this the out-of-the-loop performance problem.

This reduced involvement may affect more than a person’s readiness to intervene. It can change the capabilities available to the organization.

What work remains for people does not necessarily become easier. It may become harder. These are the situations where experience and independent judgment matter most. The result is a paradox: People may be called upon to exercise independent judgment less often, even as the judgments left to them become more difficult.

The accountability problem

Accountability may not change as quickly as the work does when organizations deploy AI systems. An employee may now oversee far more decisions than they make themselves, while remaining responsible for the outcomes. The organization’s expectations may still reflect how the work was divided before AI took on a larger role. The organization can therefore end up holding people accountable for decisions over which they have less control.

This creates a mismatch. Research on meaningful human control suggests that responsibility should match a person’s authority and ability to act. An employee may retain the authority to override an AI recommendation and remain responsible for the outcome, yet lose the capability to do so. Authority, responsibility, and capability can begin to separate.

Latent risk becomes an organizational design problem, not simply a human performance problem.

The measurement problem

Organizations typically judge AI-enabled processes by measures such as accuracy and productivity. Those numbers may look good even as the human role is changing. Suppose employees override AI recommendations less frequently over time. Is that a sign of growing dependence? Perhaps.

But it could also mean that the AI has become more accurate and there is less reason to intervene. The number of overrides alone tells little about whether employees remain ready to exercise their own judgment.

The key is to understand how the division of work between people and AI is changing. Which decisions have migrated from people to AI? What responsibilities remain with people? Looking at the performance of the employee or the AI separately may miss what is changing between them.

The governance problem

Organizational governance—defining roles and responsibilities—is also under pressure from AI.

Someone may remain formally in the loop with an AI system even as their actual role changes. Defining human and AI roles when a system is introduced is only a starting point. As AI improves and people become accustomed to using it, those roles are likely to change over time. There is nothing inherently wrong with that change.

The problem arises when the relationship changes but the assumptions surrounding it do not. It’s important for organizations to periodically ask: What relationship between people and AI did we design, and what relationship do we actually have today?

In short, organizational governance needs to be dynamic.

Maintaining the human backstop

Not every human capability needs to be preserved. If AI can perform a task well, there is little reason to require people to keep doing the same work. Organizations need to decide which capabilities they still expect people to have when human judgment is required. If people may still be called upon to use a capability, it needs to be maintained.

Overseeing AI is not the same as exercising independent judgment. If people rarely make the decision themselves, the organization cannot assume they will be ready when they need to. One way to test this is to occasionally ask employees to make a decision without first seeing the AI recommendation. The organization needs to know that the human backstop it relies on will actually work when needed.

As AI takes on more work, some human capabilities will inevitably be used less often. Some may no longer matter. Others may still be essential when AI reaches its limits. The challenge is knowing the difference and making that choice deliberately.

For me, the central question is this: Which human capabilities does an organization still depend on, and will they be there when needed?

Murugan Anandarajan is a professor of decision sciences and management information systems at Drexel University.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] My PIP worked. My job still didn’t
items.content_html:
The day I got put on my performance improvement plan (or PIP) in my content marketing job, I drove back to an Appalachian folk magic store I’d happened into the weekend prior. I bought a bottle of Boss Fix Oil, a “conjuring oil” touted as a way of “improving work dynamics.”

I’m not a particularly spiritual man, but I truly was at my wit’s end. I’d been in this role for nearly a year, and in my 25 years of working, I’d never struggled this badly to prove my professional worth. 

A little Googling—and texts from friends—produced the same verdict: PIPs mean they’re trying to get rid of you. Start looking for new employment. 

Needless to say, I was freaking out. But I buckled down, kept my confidence and worked hard through the PIP—and yet? There was something that was bothering me beyond just the PIP. 

Getting put on one made me accept something I was struggling to: the fact that I simply didn’t fit into the culture there.

The “Culture Fit” of It All

The term “culture fit” is divisive in corporate spaces, and understandably so: It introduces subjectivity into a world that likes to pretend it’s a meritocracy. But I also think you can’t overstate the importance of fit in the workplace. A 2023 research review found organizational fit has a much stronger relationship with job satisfaction than job performance. 

The workplace is many things. Objective isn’t always one of them.

I suspected pretty early on that the way I worked and the way this company worked didn’t align. I remember talking to my mother after attending an in-person department summit for the first time. “Everyone was nice enough,” I told her. “But I feel like we approach things very differently.”

I’d tried to get most of my work done ahead of the summit so that, during our downtime, I could participate in the kind of small talk Zoom calls and Slack just don’t facilitate. But during those times? Heads were down, dutifully typing away, and conversations stuck to strategy. Even at our team happy hour, the conversations kept coming back to work projects. My perception? It felt performative—a contest to see who was most devoted.

There were other traits I didn’t fully align with. It was a workplace where climbing the corporate ladder sometimes seemed to take precedence, and navigating office politics seemed more prudent than simply doing good work.

But the big differentiator—and what I suspect ultimately led to my PIP—was what details mattered most. I’m a bigger-picture guy, more concerned with a piece of content’s angle, takeaway, and value to its audience than whether it uses curly or straight quotation marks (something that was apparently important at this job). 

By the time I was put on the PIP, I spent less time thinking strategically and more time stressed about whether an em dash or a semicolon would warrant another talk with my manager about “attention to detail.”

But I didn’t leave. I stayed and worked through the PIP. After all, I’d been laid off a year earlier and had blown through my savings; this new job was a big pay increase I convinced myself I needed. 

But I also wanted to prove I could succeed. I wanted to show I was the kind of guy who could work in tough environments. I think that’s part of why I became so determined to beat the PIP.  

Corporate culture lionizes the person who can “work with anyone,” “thrive in any environment,” and “adapt to changing priorities.” “Agility” and “flexibility” are worn as badges of honor. I’d internalized that. Being good at my job meant being malleable. 

And, frankly, I’d failed at one of the most important aspects of any job: reading the room. I knew my approach differed from the company’s, yet I’d been overconfident in my own. Leaving felt like admitting I couldn’t hack it.

Success Is Subjective 

The easier piece to write—and frankly, the piece my id still wants to—positions me as the victim of the dreaded toxic workplace, the aggrieved creative just trying to do good work somewhere that prized a degree of precision I sometimes found superfluous. But I’ve been deliberately using qualifiers like “my perception” and “estimation” because one person’s toxic could be another person’s ideal.

At a job that was a great fit for me, I remember turning in my first piece of writing and apologizing when a member of upper management had to fix a few typos. 

And yet? “We all make typos,” she told me. “If all I have to do is clean up a few small ones, but the stories are good? You’re excelling.” Plus, at that company’s in-person summit, she started a happy-hour conversation with, “No work talk.” 

That was my favorite job. And it’s 100% the toxic job in someone else’s story: While I liked its informal, collaborative, and relatively unstructured environment (we worked from home and had a lot of freedom in setting our own schedules), there were colleagues—people who thrived with more structure or preferred more hierarchical, competitive environments—who weren’t a good fit.

I don’t believe in magic. I do believe in reframing your thinking. 

So when I Googled ways to optimize conjuring oil use back at the job that served me the PIP, I found a Reddit comment that advised using it with an open mind. It reminded me of another comment I’d found (I’m paraphrasing) during my earlier PIP Googling: “PIPs often aren’t about the quality of your work. They’re about you not fitting in.”

Whether or not that’s the most common truth behind PIPs, I did something I probably should’ve done earlier. I swallowed my pride. It didn’t matter if I thought fixating on quotation marks or putting on a show of productivity was ridiculous. It mattered that this workplace valued it.

Beating the PIP

So, I made myself malleable. And a week into my four-week PIP, things already felt like they were turning around: I focused on the small details. I executed new initiatives without question. I thanked my manager profusely for sharpening my editorial eye and made sure to talk about my “working lunches.”

I passed my PIP with flying colors. 

The month afterward was probably the most aligned I felt with the company since coming on board. I felt like I was making real contributions. I felt like I fit in. 

Was I happy and thriving? I wouldn’t say that. I was the one performing now. And I don’t know—for me, at least—how sustainable that would’ve been. 

I never got to find out.

A month after passing my PIP, en route to an outdoor weekend in Shenandoah National Park for a friend’s 40th—and what felt, a bit, like a victory lap after a stressful Q3—I got a text asking me to check my email and log into a Zoom call about “structural changes that are impacting your role at the organization.” I was laid off in the waiting area of a Virginia rest stop.

My department head assured me it had nothing to do with my performance. Everyone had been very impressed with my recent efforts. This was a business decision. Nothing more.

I believe them. Not only because they wrote me a glowing letter of recommendation, but because I know I’m good at content marketing. Just maybe not . . . there. I also know now that there’s no magic cure for a bad fit. After all, a 2026 survey found that 62% of workers said adopting a professional persona helped their careers, but 65% said doing so drained their energy or motivation.

I think that’s what surprised me most about the whole experience. The PIP worked. I changed the ways I was approaching my job, figured out what was expected of me, and proved I could deliver. 

Even if I disagreed with what this workplace valued, I still had something to learn from it. In fact, I’ve carried some of those lessons into my current job, where I’m noticeably more attentive to details that old me would’ve considered nitpicky. I even value them more. 

But I also think there’s a difference between being capable of succeeding somewhere and being somewhere you can succeed as yourself. I spent nearly a year trying to overcome what I now recognize as incompatibilities, convinced that if I just worked harder or became more adaptable, I’d eventually feel like I belonged. 

And maybe that’s the lesson I’d offer anyone facing a PIP: Take the feedback seriously. Make the changes you need to make. But don’t confuse proving you can do a job with proving it’s the right job for you. And don’t be afraid to admit when something isn’t working and proactively change course. 

I have three-quarters of the bottle of Boss Fix Oil left. Just in case.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] What actually motivates AI talent to work for companies
items.content_html:
Mark Zuckerberg hand-delivered homemade soup to OpenAI researchers’ front doors in an attempt to recruit them. Elon Musk pledged to personally read every SpaceX AI application—no résumé required; pedigree optional. When the world’s richest founders are cold-calling engineers with soup and big-figure job offers, it’s clear the AI talent war has reached a new, absurd level.

But Meta and SpaceX aren’t the only ones taking outlandish measures to attract talent in the tightest hiring market in tech history. The median base salary for startup engineers is $200,000, a 25% increase since 2022 and a far cry from the equity-first model that startups have relied on for decades. 

Artificial intelligence roles are taking a long time to fill, and there are plenty of them. AI, machine learning, and data science postings jumped 163% in 2025 from 2024, yet 72% of employers say they’re struggling to fill roles. The challenge isn’t just supply. It’s also a hiring strategy issue. The old model of a charismatic founder with a vision—and often no product yet—is out. AI talent wants to see hard proof, not a pitch deck. 

What AI talent responds to

I recently published research on how founders and AI specialists interact on CoffeeSpace, a platform focused on helping startups build early teams from cofounder matching to recruitment. The matching works like a dating app; users send invitations the same way you swipe on Tinder or Hinge. Except instead of singles searching for a match, founders and engineers decide whether to accept or decline an invitation to start a conversation. Of its roughly 25,000 users and 1 million swipes, we narrowed the analysis to 6,868 people involved in AI-relevant matches—357 of whom qualified as AI talent— across about 160,000 decisions.  

I found a disconnect between what founders think AI talent wants, and what AI talent is actually looking for.

Founder ambition and equity offers aren’t enough to pique a candidate’s interest anymore. Instead, AI specialists want to see momentum. Founders working full-time on their project were 20% more likely to have their invitations accepted than those still in the exploration phase. But momentum doesn’t require a finished product. A prototype and a handful of early users can signal that an idea has traction, which AI specialists want to see.

A PhD, an MBA, or a stint at Meta or Google used to matter. Today, they are weaker predictors than most founders assume. AI professionals are seeking out founders with nontechnical backgrounds. Founders with legal experience saw 18% higher acceptance rates; those with sales experience saw a 10% lift. 

The reasoning tracks. A founder with a legal background can lower perceived risks around compliance, IP, and contracts. A sales background demonstrates that a founder knows how to get products in front of paying customers, not just investors. Any professional experience outside of tech can signal to talent that this founder will let them focus on building, rather than reviewing investor decks.

Of course, AI specialists also make decisions based on compensation, equity, and remote work options, but later in the process than founders might realize. Perks like these don’t create interest on their own, but they can remove friction for candidates who are already in the negotiation stage.

What founders can do about it

Most founders can’t compete with Zuckerberg’s theatrics or Musk’s budget. The good news is that the data suggests they don’t need to.

People looking for top AI talent can make progress visible. Publishing a build log, sharing a demo video, or putting a working prototype in front of even a handful of users before recruiting begins can demonstrate momentum.

If a team is heavy on technical expertise, it may help to hire people with legal or sales experience before stacking the team with another engineer. Having a coworker with experience in these fields can do more to attract AI talent. And save the perks conversation for later, as flexible compensation and remote work options close deals rather than opening them.

AI pros want a viable prototype more than a soup delivery. They’d rather be left to work on the product than get sucked into strategy meetings. They want committed founders, not a Steve Jobs-like visionary running on charisma alone. In short, they want proof that what they’re building is real, and that the people building it are grounded. No amount of soup can make up for that.

items.title: [Théoo] My phone is a noisy place
items.content_html:
A while back, I shared a note about how I had cut down my phone usage a lot and what it had changed for me.

And for a few months, I actually stuck to it.
But lately, I've been watching or listening to videos from the moment I wake up to the moment I go to sleep. And for the times when I can't watch videos (like when I'm walking in the street, for example), I will put a podcast or music to occupy the space.

I'm not sure why I went back to this sluggish state when I had been doing so well for a long time, but I think it's because I actually missed watching specific YouTubers and listening to specific podcasts. So I allowed some back into my life and then some more and eventually, it took over.

Which leaves me in a weird situation, because I now know that no YouTube at all is disappointing. There is some content that I actually like and don't want to stop watching, especially since it's only like at most 2 hours per week plus the occasional GeoWizard adventure.
But at the same time, I know that if I let these back in, I won't be able to stop myself, because there is a ton of content that I like, content that I wouldn't miss if I didn't watch it, but that is still nice to watch.
I could try an extension to hide the recommendations, but knowing me, I will probably deactivate it pretty quickly and find an "acceptable" reason why. Worth a try though, I guess.

The other thing that crept back is Spotify. I listen to music (or podcasts, but mostly music) when I'm not watching videos. On the one hand, it's great because I have discovered many new artists lately, but at the same time, I've been feeling more disconnected, irritated when someone is trying to talk to me and I have to remove my AirPods and, overall like my mind can never breathe.
I'd say that the thing that has changed since the last article is that now silence isn't weird anymore. I even enjoy it! But for some reason I always feel this need to listen to something. Plus, I have been questioning my relationship with music lately, but I will talk about it in another note.

Now again, I'm not sure about what the right thing to do is. I definitely don't want to stop listening to music, I enjoy it way too much. But I don't want it to be constant.
Trying to apply time restrictions won't work because I know that I will find "good reasons" to circumvent them.
Maybe something like "you can only listen to music when you do this and that" could work. This has worked for podcasts already, as there are some podcasts that I only listen to when cleaning and others I only listen to when grocery shopping.
Another idea would be to say "You can only listen to music out loud" and not in your AirPods. So that would automatically limit my time, because there are many situations where you can't listen to music out loud.

So where does this leave me? What about the things I said in the previous note about enjoying life without all this?
I guess it's as with all things in life, I need to find balance.

The approach to ditch all music and YouTube was certainly too extreme, but spending my whole days listening to stuff is also too extreme.
Another thing to consider is the fact that I tend to get absorbed by things, both the good and the bad ones.
So when I get to reading a book or programming something, I will just do it for hours upon hours to the point of forgetting to eat. But the same can be said for playing video games and watching videos, which has a much more negative impact.
And I don't know that I should change this, it's just a part of my personality, but I need to learn to put systems in place to prevent it for things that make me rot away.

I don't have a good conclusion yet. Honestly, I think that what would help me would be to have the opinions from a bunch of different people and see how they deal with all this, to try as many options as possible until I find the balance I'm looking for.

For now, I will try to limit Spotify and I will try YouTube "blocking" extensions. If you have any other ideas or want to share your experience, please email me, I'd be grateful to receive it.

I hope you have a great day, bye.

items.title: [blog.mastykarz.nl] Be honest about what your evals prove
items.content_html:
Your coding agent just scored 100% on an eval, and every criterion passed. There's only one problem: the code it generated doesn't build. How is that possible? The eval checked 20 aspects of the implementation. The agent used the right APIs and followed the expected patterns. It created the required files and included the necessary configuration. Every one of those checks passed, but nobody tried building the application.

The eval did exactly what it was designed to do. It verified the criteria it was given, and the agent met all of them. The problem starts with what we infer from that result. A 100% eval score means that 100% of the evaluated criteria passed. It doesn't tell you whether the agent completed the user's task.

The temptation of proxies

Ideally, an eval verifies whether the agent achieved the user's goal. If the user asks for a working application, you verify that the application works. In practice, that's easier said than done. Consider evaluating an agent that builds and deploys a cloud application. To verify that it succeeded, you'd need to build the generated code and provision the infrastructure. Then you'd deploy the application and exercise its functionality before cleaning everything up. Along the way, you'd have to handle failures and unpredictable outputs, sometimes for applications whose implementation you can't anticipate. A harness like that can take considerable time and money to build.

So we compromise. Instead of verifying that the application works, we check whether the generated code looks plausible. We inspect the files and configuration that the agent produced and compare its API usage against the patterns we expect. These checks become proxies for functional success, and there's nothing inherently wrong with that. Engineering is full of tradeoffs, and evaluating agents is no exception. Sometimes direct verification is impractical, and a proxy is the best evidence you can reasonably get. The trap is forgetting that we're measuring a proxy and communicating the result as proof of success.

Validation isn't the same as success

Agent skills show the same pattern. You can automatically verify that a skill's frontmatter is valid and that its structure follows the specification. You can even check whether the agent invokes the skill or whether its output contains certain strings. These checks are useful because they catch structural problems and regressions, much like linting or static analysis does in traditional software development. But none of them prove that the skill helps the agent complete the user's task.

Nobody claims that an application works because it passes linting. We treat static analysis and builds as different evidence from functional tests, and we validate performance and deployments separately again, because each of them tells us something different about the software. Agent evaluations deserve the same discipline. A skill that passes structural validation meets certain technical requirements. An agent invoking the skill is evidence that the skill was invoked. That's it. Neither, on its own, proves that the user got what they asked for, and even a comprehensive collection of proxy checks might miss the one thing that matters most.

What does your eval actually prove?

Before you publish an eval result, complete this sentence, and be precise about it:

When this eval passes, we know that…

If your eval checks implementation patterns without building the code, an honest answer sounds like this:

When this eval passes, we know that the agent generated code that satisfies our implementation criteria. We haven't verified that it builds or runs.

That's a defensible claim. What you shouldn't say is that the agent built a working application, because your eval never checked that. The same goes for the cloud application from earlier. An agent can generate infrastructure definitions and deployment scripts that look entirely correct, but until you deploy and validate the application, you don't know whether it works in the target environment. If a working deployment was what the user asked for, that's a significant gap in your evidence. An eval doesn't have to verify everything. You might deliberately accept that gap because direct verification costs too much, and that's your tradeoff to make. But the confidence you communicate should never exceed the evidence you've collected.

Don't let the nuance disappear

Imagine a team that reports consistently high eval scores. The results look excellent. Management sees progress that justifies the investment, and everyone believes that the agent experience is improving. Meanwhile, users complain that the generated applications don't work. How can both be true? Perhaps the eval scenarios don't represent what users actually encounter, or the criteria verify implementation details while missing functional failures. Perhaps both. Either way, the team has been optimizing against its eval results while gradually losing touch with what its users experience.

That's why a misleading eval can be worse than no eval at all. Without evidence, you know that you're uncertain. With a reassuring score that nobody fully understands, you might stop asking whether things actually work. So when users report failures despite high eval scores, treat that as a reason to revisit both your scenarios and your criteria. Your eval might cover different situations from the ones your users face, or measure outcomes other than the ones they care about.

Preventing this is primarily the job of the people who design the evals. They know what they measured and which compromises they made, so they also know what remains unverified. You can't expect everyone who reads the results to inspect the eval harness and reconstruct those limitations themselves. You can report them in a matrix of separate scores or in a short explanation. Either works, as long as the scope and limitations of the evidence travel with the results.

Be deliberate about what you measure

Proxies are often a practical response to how complex it is to evaluate real-world agent behavior. They're still compromises, though, and you should make them deliberately. Whenever possible, evaluate whether the user actually succeeded. When that's impractical, use the best evidence you can get and be clear about its limitations. Don't confuse validation checks with outcome evaluations, and don't let a perfect score imply more than you've verified. Before you celebrate your next 100% eval score, ask yourself: when this eval passes, what do we actually know? Then make sure that's also what everyone reading the results understands.

items.title: [Théoo] On techno-solutionism
items.content_html:
I've been seeing more techno-solutionist talk online lately. Maybe it's just my algorithms that decided to show me more of that or maybe people are actually talking more about it. Either way, it made me think about this subject and it's implications, and also made me quite scared.

When I talk about techno-solutionism in this post, I mean it in relation towards climate change. Here's a definition to make sure we're all thinking about the same thing when reading this article.

Techno-solutionism is the idea that we will fix the climate crisis by using technology so we don't have to change our way of life.

Now let me preface by saying that I personally don't believe in techno-solutionism and I will develop why in this post. But even if you believe in it, I think you should read-on as my goal is not to judge or critisize but rather to ask questions and I think your answers would be as interesting as anyone else's.

The solutions that are often brought up in techno-solutionist discussions are Carbon Capture, AGI that will find the solutions for us, Geoengineering and Nuclear fusion.
As of now, none of these solutions are a reality. We are seeing progress in each of them, but they still pose many challenges that we are yet so solve.

The question then is, do we want to bet on things that we don't know for sure will ever become a reality? Because, you might strongly believe these will someday exist but you can't prove that they will. It's just a belief.
Personally, I don't want to throw the life of future generations of living beings to a bet.

Now, let's say this works and we actually figure these things out! What tells us that we'll figure them out in time?

Because while we are working on these solutions, the climate crisis is still going on. Living beings are quickly dying and becoming extinct, and even if you don't care about non-human forms of life, humans are dying too.

Are we as a species really willing to let so many other forms of life die for us to keep up with our current way of life?

Are we, the people living in privileged countries willing to keep exploiting other humans for our own profit and well being?

And can we really feel well and happy about how we'll live in a world where we have "fixed" the climate crisis but can still feel all the damages it caused?

Maybe your answer to all of these is yes, and maybe you'd even tell me that it's also possible that we will figure techno-solutions in time.
So let's say you are right about this, let's say that by 2050, we've found solutions that allow us to go to negative carbon emissions!

Then the question is, are you willing to let companies decide of the quality of the air you breathe?
Because since we live in a capitalist society, the companies running carbon capture machines and doing the geoengineering required to keep our current living standards will want to make profit.

They won't do it for the sake of being nice to us, when is the last time you've seen a company just be nice and gain profit off of it?

Now you could argue that we are already trusting companies for many really important things like electricity or transport of goods. But these aren't vital things.
People used to live without electricity and they would grow their own food, but no one would be able to live without breathable air.

My personal opinion on this is that I am definitely not ok with putting my survival and the survival of future generations in the hands of any company. And don't get me wrong, I would love to keep up the life that I currently have, it's so comfortable. And I so wish that every human going forward would have the same comfort of life that I have. But I simply don't think it is possible.

Maybe you are ok with the idea that only a few living beings will have a great life at the cost of all others, in which case, business as usual is perfectly fine. But I am not.

I believe that it is more than overdue that we start rethinking our future.
I don't want of a future where machines are what is keeping us alive like we are some sort of ill person surviving only because of their ventilator.

Let's use what we know and are sure of to build a new collective imagination. A world where yes, we will have lost a lot of our current comfort at the benefit of more equality, more mutual aid, more connexion to nature and each other, more time to think and dream.
A world where we can wake up every day without being stressed by an imminent wall that we seem to being sprinting towards at great speeds.

Sure, we won't be able to eat McDonalds, order stuff from the other side of the world for only a couple bucks and get it delivered the same day, drive a car to go buy food at the big nearby mall, travel for a few hundred euros/dollars to go virtually anywhere in at most 2 days, change phone as we please, etc

But isn't that worth it for the certainty that we and other livings, will be able to live for millennia to come?

We should stop being trapped in our current vision of the world and I'm hopeful that someday we'll look back on this time period like we are looking back on how they lived in the middle ages.

I would love to hear about you opinion on this subject, even if you disagree. So please feel free to send me a mail so we can discuss this matter further.

Have a nice day :))

The argument here, stated about half way through the post, is that "when content becomes abundant, judgment becomes scarce." So "that is where learning professionals can bring more value." Let's think about that. A while ago I proposed a type of AI, called "deontic analytics", would decide what is worthwhile, what is valuable, what should be done. I've seen nothing that suggests AI will be incapable of this. Why would we trust human judgement over AI, if AI can be demonstrably better at this? Consider the new decision models, like Jev and Clef and Decision 1.0 (I'll be a human named that one). It's not obvious that human judgement will always be better. Image: Shadhin.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] AI fear is driving employees to slack off, show up late, and even steal coworkers’ lunches
items.content_html:
🌾 🪶 ✏️

As more businesses adopt artificial intelligence, some employees—who are increasingly worried about losing their jobs—are starting to act out.

That’s the finding of a new study from Washington State University researchers, published in the journal Occupational Health Science, that looks at how AI adoption at work is affecting workers’ attitudes and behaviors in the office.

Research has shown that the increase of AI-based technologies at work—such as intelligent robotics, automated systems, and algorithmic management—may make employees feel insecure about their jobs and lead to more stress and less engagement.

Washington State University’s study looked at employees across 18 different industries and found that workers who had the greatest fears about being replaced by AI were more likely to behave poorly by, for example, slacking off at the office or even stealing a coworker’s lunch.

Researchers also found that employees who assumed they would be displaced were more likely to “morally disengage” at work, such as by coming in late for a shift or surfing the web while on the clock.

“Moral disengagement is basically a way of justifying bad behavior,” Tahira M. Probst, a professor of psychology at WSU Vancouver and lead author of the study, said in a news release. “We know what’s right and wrong. We know what organizational policies say we can and can’t do. Moral disengagement is a way of reframing that behavior as something that is acceptable.”

Researchers used the AI Industry Exposure index to identify which industries were most exposed to potential AI disruption. Workers in finance and insurance had some of the highest levels of exposure, while workers in agriculture, forestry, and construction had the least. Not surprisingly, the bad behavior was more pronounced in the industries with the highest amount of disruption.

The study’s bottom line: When employees feel their jobs are at risk, they may look at workplace expectations differently and rationalize behaviors such as cutting corners or undermining coworkers to protect themselves or compensate for what they perceive as injustice.

The findings also suggest that AI anxieties can hurt workers and businesses alike, pointing to the need for employers to be more mindful of how they roll out AI in the workplace so employees are better supported.
